title.en: Night and Darkness and Their Three Daughters

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I: Mitologie en legendes (1919), No. 2

summary.en: Before sun, moon or stars there was only twilight. 'Ga (Night) and 'Gagen (Darkness) lived in a rock cave with three daughters, each wearing a magic rattle-string — of tortoise shells, of gourd shells, of springbok-ear bladders — forbidden ever to remove. 'Kaggen, the Mantis, watched their dances as a great buck; the father shot him; the quarters came alive, rejoined, and the 'Hotnotsgod' ran off. Then he sent three sons as suitors, and the girls, wed, became the mothers of plenty.
summary.zh: 日月星未生，天地僅餘微明。'加（夜）與'加根（暗）居石穴，育三女，各佩魔鈴串——龜殼、葫蘆殼、跳羚耳囊——戒令永不可解。螳螂卡根化大羚觀舞，父射之；肉塊復活，節節自合，卡根遁走。後遣三子求婚，三女既嫁，豐饒自茲始。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh from named Bushman narrators of the Hantam and Hartebeest rivers, 1870s-1880s; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
Von Wielligh's narrators were emphatic: everything was born from darkness. First it was evening, and then morning. In the old days there was only a dim twilight, like a heavy overcast day; it was cold, and the Sun, the Moon and the Stars did not yet shine. Old 'Ga (Night) and his wife 'Gagen (Darkness) lived in a rock cave. They had no sons, only three daughters.

When the three girls grew up, the mother made them rattling necklaces. For the eldest she took little tortoise shells, hollowed them, dropped pebbles inside so they would rattle, and strung them on a bobbejaan-skin thong; she forbade the girl ever to take it off, or the food in her belly would perish. For the second she strung little gourd shells filled with berry-seeds on a cord of inner bark; for the youngest she took springbok ears, made little bladders of the white inner pit, dried them with sand and filled them with the hard grains that lie inside springbok eyes, strung on springbok sinew. Each daughter wore her commandment: never remove the string.

The father and mother called the girls to dance before the people, and many came from far to see them; the young men were wary of the three dancers, for they held them to be witch-people. 'Kaggen — the Mantis, whom the narrators call the 'Hotnotsgod' — sat on a bush watching and listening day after day. To see better he changed himself into a great wild buck and came close. The old father seized his quiver and bow, stalked the great buck, shot and hit it; the buck ran a little way and fell — or rather, pretended to fall.

The family walked up to cut it up. The father carried a hindquarter and the skin, the mother the other hindquarter and the inner parts, the eldest daughter a forequarter, the second the other forequarter, and the youngest the head with the backbone. The head began to talk, to groan piteously, and to wink its eyes. Three times the youngest girl called out that the buck's head was still alive; the others laughed her off. At the third call the carriers stood still — and the four quarters turned on the carriers' heads. In terror they set them down on bushes; each quarter sprang up, ran to the backbone, and fastened itself to its place; the entrails crept back in; the skin folded itself around; and the buck stood again before them, calm. It gave a short gallop away and became the Mantis once more. So the old father and his family found that 'Kaggen had cheated them.

Not content, the Mantis after some days changed three of his sons into three young men and sent them to woo the three daughters. The girls fell in love with the fine young men and married them; they built huts of bushes and lived there, for game and veld food abounded — as their mother had foretold — so long as the daughters wore the rattle-strings. Other Bushmen came to live there and hunt, and the place became a place of pleasure: no quarrels, food and all needs in abundance. In one word, it was a lazy-sweet land.

functions: Cosmogony: night and darkness as the primal parents of the habitable world.
Explains the power of rattling necklaces (tortoise, gourd, springbok-ear) as life-giving amulets.
Reinforces the Mantis's role as undying deceiver even of Night's own family.

variants.name: |Xam 'Children of Night' parallels
variants.summary: The |Xam tell of an early race that could change at will into animals; von Wielligh's Hantam narrators give the same shape-shifting premise in a domestic cosmogony.

variants.name: Kaggen's eland deception parallel
variants.summary: The self-rejoining buck quarters echo the self-rejoining hartebeest the Mantis feigned in Specimens.

title.en: The Mountains Are the Eldest Daughter

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I: Mitologie en legendes (1919), No. 3

summary.en: 'Kou, Night's eldest daughter, weds a son of the Mantis and grows tortoise-lazy; a bobbejaan demands her tortoise-shell necklace — made of his brother's skin — and returns with a commando. The Mantis changes his son into a great bird and the child into the Echo; the whirlwind fells the raiders, who swear to trample her grave and roll its stones forever. 'Kou sleeps and sleeps, and has become the mountains.
summary.zh: '口——夜之長女——嫁螳螂之子，因嗜龜肉而懶惰。狒狒索其龜殼鈴串——云係其兄弟之皮——率眾來襲。螳螂化子為巨鳥、化童為回聲；旋風摧敵，敗者誓踏其墓、永滾其石。'口長眠不醒，遂成群山。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
'Kou, the eldest of Night's three daughters, married a son of the 'Hotnotsgod (the Mantis); they built huts of bushes. Never taking off her tortoise-shell necklace, she could catch tortoises as she pleased — but she grew so fond of tortoise flesh that she wanted nothing else, and, like the slow, lazy tortoise, she grew slow and lazy herself. A short walk to fetch tortoises took her nearly the whole day; she did nothing more for husband or child. Her husband scolded, then beat her — as well have scolded a tortoise, or rattled the pebbles in the shells. He had to do everything alone, even catch her tortoises.

One day, while he was away hunting, a bobbejaan came and asked the child where her mother was: he wanted the thong that bound the tortoise shells on her neck, for it was made of the skin of his brother. The child would not tell; the bobbejaan threatened to come next day and tear the necklace from 'Kou's neck by force. When the father came home the child begged him to stay; next day the bobbejaan came as promised, and the husband threatened him with bow and arrow. The bobbejaan warned that he would return with a commando of his brothers and break the huts to flinders.

The husband hurried out to gather food and made ready for the attack. As promised, the bobbejaan came with a great company of his family. The Mantis, watching quietly from a bush, changed his son into a great bird and the child into the Echo. The bird rose and made a great wind with its wings; thick dust arose, and the Echo made a great noise. As the bird wheeled, a terrible whirlwind arose, hurling stones and pieces of wood; here a bobbejaan took a stone on the head, there another a blow with a stick, and the sand and dust blinded them so that they scattered and fled.

From far off they called back: 'Wait, we will never leave 'Kou in peace — over her grave we will walk, and the stones of it we will turn and roll forever.' But they slunk away. And 'Kou grew lazier by the day: she fell asleep, and slept, and slept to this very day. In her sleep she became a great mountain, never to wake again. When the bobbejaans saw her become mountains they were only glad; in revenge they walk on the mountains and roll the stones, as they swore. 'Kou, the mountains, is not dead: she only rests in an eternal sleep.

functions: Origin of mountains as the sleeping body of Night's eldest daughter.
Explains the bobbejaan's habit of turning and rolling stones on high places.
Charter for the echo as a child-spirit that answers from the rocks.

variants.name: Plains sister parallel (No. 6)
variants.summary: The second daughter 'Kaun sleeps likewise and becomes the plains; her necklace's seeds root through her throat.

variants.name: Waters sister parallel (No. 9)
variants.summary: The youngest daughter becomes the restless waters; the springbok raid brings rain and flood.

summary.en: 'Kou's husband, the Mantis's son, became the Wind-bird and dwells in a hole in the cliffs; near it no one goes. If angered he flings people down, whirls them into the sky, strips their huts and carries off the mats. He was once a man of the old race; now when he flaps slowly the wind blows soft, when he beats the ground a dust-storm rises. He is also the breath in living things: take away his wind and a person dies.
summary.zh: '口之夫——螳螂之子——化為風鳥，居於崖穴；近其穴者不得。怒則擲人於地、捲人上天、拆其屋掠其席。他本是古族之人；今其緩拍則微風，拍地則沙暴。又為萬物之氣息：奪其風者死。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 4 (1919); not verbatim. 'Kou's husband, the son of the 'Hotnotsgod, was changed into a bird, the Wind-bird, and went to live in a hole in a rock cliff. No one goes near the hole where the wind lives; out of it blows a violent wind that flings a person to the ground and fills his eyes with sand and dust — or the whirlwind lifts him up into the sky, carries him far away, and lets him fall from above.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Wind was first a man of the old race; he walked and played and hunted like the others. Now that he is a bird, when he flaps his wings slowly the wind blows gently; when he beats the ground with his feet and whips up the sand, the dust rises in banks, the trees bend and crack, and the storm flattens everything it touches.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The Wind-bird sends his wind into people and animals too; when he takes away the wind of a person or animal, that one dies, and no breath ever comes again into mouth and nostrils. So one must beware of naming the bird's name, or of speaking badly of him when he is near — two children who shot and threw stones at him were caught by the whirlwind, spun like tops, and driven fleeing from trees to rocks to a cave, until their mothers burned sweet-smelling bushes and strewed buchu into the wind, and sang it calm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 4; not verbatim.

title.en: The Echo, Daughter of the Mountains

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 5

summary.en: The Echo is the mountains' daughter; her father is the Wind speaking through her. Speelman, first inventor of music — kudu-horn trumpets, reed flutes, gut-stringed ramkies and a pot-drum — follows her singing into the kloofs, is lured apart voice by voice until lost among lions, wolves and jackals, escapes a lion by feigning death, and escapes the bobbejaans by blowing his horn till the cliffs thunder.
summary.zh: 回聲為山之女；其父乃風，借其口而言。斯皮爾曼——樂之始創者——聞其歌而入深谷，聲音漸分漸遠，迷失於獅、狼、豺之間；佯死脫獅，吹號震崖，驚走狒狒。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 5 (1919); not verbatim. The Echo, or Echo, is the daughter of the mountains — her father is the Wind, who speaks through her daughter. She is a mocker who is never tired: the one she teases will weary and grow angry, but the Echo never. She lives in the deep kloofs among the cliffs and precipices, and she sleeps never; when anyone calls, she answers at once — she is always awake.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. The man who first invented music was named Speelman. He made trumpets from kudu horns, flutes from flute-reed, stringed instruments from the sinews of wild animals, and even a drum from a pot with a springbok skin stretched over it. Speelman could sing and play so beautifully that he sought for one who could sing and play as beautifully as he; and the people told him of a girl in the kloofs whose name was Echo.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He blew his kudu horn and began to sing, and was astonished that the Echo sang more beautifully still, for an echo always sounds finer than the voice it answers. But the nearer he came the further the voices moved apart — one voice, then two, then three, then more — until he wandered into the gramadoelas, the wild mountains, lost. He escaped the bobbejaans by blowing his great horn till the kloofs thundered, the lion by playing dead while it carried him, and after long wandering he reached his home.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 5; not verbatim.

title.en: The Plains Are the Second Daughter

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 6

summary.en: 'Kaun, Night's second daughter, weds the Mantis's son and grows drowsy on her gourd-necklace of seeds; a Tree comes for the necklace strung on his brother's inner bark, then a whole wood. The Mantis changes his son into a great Fire and the child into the Mirage; the trees flee, swearing to root into her grave. 'Kaun sleeps and has become the plains, with bushes and grass rooted in her throat.
summary.zh: '昆——夜之次女——嫁螳螂之子，因葫蘆鈴串之籽而慵倦；樹來索其串——謂係其兄弟之內皮——後舉林而至。螳螂化子為烈火、化童為蜃景；群樹奔逃，誓根入其墓。'昆長眠成平原；灌木草芥根入其喉。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 6 (1919); not verbatim. The second daughter of 'Ga and 'Gagen, 'Kaun, went with her husband to live in huts of matjiesgoed; she was very clever at making mats. The bewitching necklace of gourd shells made many kinds of plants and fruits grow around her, so that there was plenty of mat-reed; but it took her appetite for meat away, and idleness came over her as over her eldest sister.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 6; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A Tree came asking for the necklace, whose cord was made of the inner bark of the trunk of his brother; the bare place on the trunk was rotting, and his brother wanted to die. Next day a whole wood came with him; the husband refused, and the trees grew riotous with a great noise. The 'Hotnotsgod changed the man into a great Fire and the child into the Mirage; the trees fled before the flames, swearing to root into her grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 6; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. 'Kaun grew lazier, felt a pain in her neck, and when she woke the seeds in the gourd shells had begun to grow and had sent their roots through her neck into her body. She became the plains and sleeps today; the trees, bushes and grass grow over her, thrusting their roots into the throat of the Earth — into 'Kaun's throat. As long as there is a world there will be plains, and as long as there are plains the bushes and grass will grow on them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 6; not verbatim.

title.en: Fire the Dancer and the 'Nu Feast

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 7

summary.en: Danser, Fire, is a son of the Mantis; his head gives light in the sunless twilight world. At a great feast he teaches fire-drilling — soft wood, whirled stick, fine grass — and a blaze that the people worship; he draws two rings about the fire, one for roasting meat (for till then people ate raw like lions and jackals) and one beyond which is the outside world, and institutes the 'Ku-dance. He still hates the trees for rooting in his wife the Plains.
summary.zh: 丹瑟（火）為螳螂之子；無日之世界中，其頭放光。大宴之上，他教鑽木取火——軟木、旋桿、細草——烈焰起而眾人拜。他以二圈圍火：內圈炙肉（自此人類始食熟，免如獅豺生食），外圈之外乃外世；並立'庫之舞。彼至今恨樹根纏其妻（平原）。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 7 (1919); not verbatim. The Fire's name is Danser, but his wife 'Kaun has been changed into the plains. He is a son of the 'Hotnotsgod and first walked like a man, hunting and playing. He still walks about like a man, but mostly one cannot see him; like his brother the Wind he creeps everywhere. Strike stones together and fire leaps out; rub sticks together and the wood kindles; lightning-fire comes out of the sky too.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Fire has crept into people and animals and plants as well: if it goes out of a person or beast the flesh grows cold and they die. At a great feast Danser taught the people to make fire: he hollowed a soft stick, laid shavings in the hollow, put fine rubbed grass beside it, and whirled a thinner harder stick upright between his flat hands until the shavings took, the grass began, and a great fire burnt up; and the people sang and danced around it in wonder.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. He drew a wide ring about the fire and bade them bring the meat inside it to roast — for until then everyone ate raw food like the lion, leopard, wolf and jackal — and the people tasted that roast meat is sweeter than raw. Then he drew a second ring outside the roasting-ring, and between the two rings the people had to dance, sing and make music. From that day feasts were held and the 'Ku-dance was instituted.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 7; not verbatim.

title.en: Antjie of the Plains: The Mirage Girl

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 8

summary.en: The mirage is the daughter of the Plains and of Fire, wordless but full of tricks, mother of dreams. When strangers overrun the Bushman country she dances above the flames — the chief's son follows and burns — then shows them glittering waters, woods and huts that shift and hang upside down, lulls them into dreams of plenty, and when they wake it is all gone and they are back where they began.
summary.zh: 蜃景乃平原與火之女，無言而多詭，夢之母。異族侵桑土，她於焰上起舞——酋長之子追之而焚——繼而現閃爍之水、林、屋，形影互易，倒懸於空；誘其入豐饒之夢；醒時萬象俱無，原地如故。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 8 (1919); not verbatim. Like the Echo, the Mirage is a mocker and lure of people in the field; she dazzles their eyes so that they see things that do not exist. The Mirage is the daughter of the Plains and of Fire; she has remained true to her parents and therefore still dances above the flame of Fire and on the Plains.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 8; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She can speak with people through dreams, for she is the mother of Dreams. When the land of the Bushmen of the old race was overrun by strong strangers of another kind, Antjie of the Plains showed herself first as a beautiful girl; the son of the strangers' leader fell in love, and she bade him do as she did: she danced above the flames of the Fire — and he, who did not yet know fire, came into the flames and was burnt. The strangers rose in wrath to kill her people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 8; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She appeared to the weary pursuers in terror-filled dreams so they could not rest; she showed them in the distance a great pan of water, beautiful woods, houses and huts — but as they walked the shapes changed: the cliffs loosened, the trees hung head-down, trees grew in the air. They fell into despair and turned back; she let them fall asleep and showed them splendid dreams of fat game and fruit; when they woke they were standing again at their old dwelling-places. So the Mirage delivered her people.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 8; not verbatim.

title.en: The Waters Are the Youngest Daughter

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 9

summary.en: 'Khwa, Night's youngest daughter, quick as a springbok by her ear-necklace, is demanded by a great Springbok who wants the sinew thong; he threatens to return with his brothers and trample her. The Mantis changes her husband into the great Rain-Beast and the child into the great Water-Snake with the shining stone on its head; mist and black rain-clouds burst, a flood drowns the raiders, and the girl becomes the restless Waters that never sleep — flowing to rivers, to the sea, and living also in men, beasts and plants.
summary.zh: '夸——夜之幼女——佩跳羚耳鈴，疾如羚；大羚索其筋弦，揚言率弟群踏之。螳螂化其夫為大雨獸、化其子為頂負閃石之大水蛇；黑雲迸發，洪水沒敵。'夸遂化為永不息之水——流為江河入海，且居於人獸草木之中。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
'Khwa, the youngest daughter, differed from her sisters. The necklace of springbok ears made her as quick as a springbok; and because a springbok does not sleep by night, she too slept little and was always restless. The necklace gave her an overpowering craving for springbok flesh, and she took great pleasure in hunting the bucks herself. Her husband also hunted, so they always had plenty for themselves and their child.

One day the child was alone at home when a great Springbok came — one of the old race. He demanded the necklace of springbok ears bound on 'Khwa's neck with springbok sinew, and stood proud and wrathful. The child would not say where her mother was and begged him to go; he answered that he would go, but would return next day with a troop of his brothers to storm 'Khwa and trample her to death if she would not give up the string. When the father came home the child told him everything, and he stayed to prepare.

Next day the dust of the approaching springboks was seen, and they grew afraid. But the Mantis, watching from a bush, changed the man into a great Ox — the Water-Beast, also called the Rain-Beast — and the child into the great Water-Snake that wears the beautiful shining stone on its head. The Rain-Beast blew a thick bank of mist from his nostrils and heavy black rain-clouds into the sky, out of which a heavy downpour fell, and a great flood of water came; and the Water-Snake let streams of water bubble up out of the ground. The springboks had to swim out and flee for their lives; they were so frightened that springboks have drunk no water since that day.

When the Rain-Beast and the Water-Snake sought 'Khwa they found that she was what had become the Waters. Because she had had little rest and was always in motion, the Waters are so too: there is always stirring and restlessness in them, like the sea. The other people tasted them and found that water takes thirst away, and from that time they drank water. But some will not drink it — the springboks, hares, tortoises and insects drink another kind of water that does not make them soon thirsty; and they will never tell where that water is to be found.

'Khwa is now the wide and restless Waters. In streams she flows to the rivers, and the rivers flow into the restless sea; in rain she floats in the clouds through the sky; as misty weather — the breath of the Rain-Beast — she sweeps over mountains and plains; she never rests; she bubbles up from the ground in fountains. The Waters, like her sisters the Mountains and the Plains, are strong: they carry great weights, and heavy things float upon them. They live not only above and below the ground, but in people, animals and plants: if they go out of them, those die of thirst. Thus Water, Fire and Wind are what keep people alive; the three do not die, and as long as there is an Earth there will be Water, Fire and Wind. Sometimes the three fight with one another — a thunderstorm means 'today Water, Fire and Wind are quarrelling again' — but mostly they work together, for if they moved out of people and animals there would be no more friendship or quarrel among them.

functions: Origin of water, rivers, rain and springs through the youngest daughter's transformation.
Explains why springbok, hare, tortoise and insects do not drink standing water.
Frames weather as the quarrel and cooperation of Water, Fire and Wind.

summary.en: In drought the bobbejaan borrows the Rain-Beast as a milk-cow, then slaughters her for the udder. A burning thirst and hunger follow: every spring dries at his lips, the ostrich eggshell of water vanishes, shade retreats. He must return and cry 'Choro, Choro, live again!' — and when he also gives back the milk-pail, the Rain-cow revives at once and a flood with locusts afloat saves him.
summary.zh: 旱時，狒狒借雨獸為乳牛，繼而殺之以取乳器。焚渴與饑隨之：泉涸、蛋殼水消、樹影退避。須返而呼「卓羅，卓羅，復活！」——歸還乳器，雨牛頓活，洪水載蝗而救其命。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 10 (1919); not verbatim. The Rain-Beast is the great rain-maker of the Bushmen; his dwelling-place is beside the great waters. In drought the people fetch him, lead him round, and show him all the places where they want rain; to put him in a good mood they dance about him, clap hands, sing, praise him and beg him to let it rain so the fields may grow green and the game and honey-bees return. He is tame if no one vexes him, and changes himself into a cow so they can milk her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 10; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. Once there was drought in the mountains where the bobbejaans lived; their leader fetched the Rain-Beast, who changed into a cow so the bobbejaan could have milk on the journey, and was milked wherever he thirsted. After he had shown every dry place he brought the Rain-cow back, and everywhere it rained beautifully. But instead of thanking her, he killed her — only to get the milk-udder to take with him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 10; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A burning thirst and gnawing hunger seized him: the green karkoere dried to dust at his touch, the fountain dried as he bent to drink, the shade shifted away from him as he walked toward it, the eggshell of water vanished at his lips. The people bade him run back and cry 'Choro, Choro, live again as you were!' and then return the milk-udder; and the Rain-cow sprang up and at once let rain fall where they stood, a flood on which banks of locusts floated. The flood rose till he sat to his neck in a tree packed with locusts, and the Rain-Beast left him there until the next day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 10; not verbatim.

title.en: The Great Water-Snake and Her Shining Stone

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 11

summary.en: The great Water-Snake, daughter of the Waters and the Rain-Beast, wears a stone on her head whose light outshines the moon at noon. She hides it before bathing; whoever steals it unseen is showered with gifts while she wastes away — until the young thief, conscience-stricken and seeing the springs run dry, restores it and wins her lasting favour.
summary.zh: 大水蛇——水與雨獸之女——頂負寶石，其光於正午猶勝月。浴前必先藏石；竊者不為所覺則受贈而蛇枯——直至少年賊良心自譴，見諸泉涸竭，歸還寶石，遂得蛇之永恩。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 11 (1919); not verbatim. The great Water-Snake can make herself great or small as she pleases; swimming up or down a river she raises the water over the banks, and lying crosswise she dams the river far back. She wears a beautiful shining stone on her head; its gleam is visible at a great distance, flashing with rays of light that surpass the light of the Moon — it can be clearly seen at midday in the brightest sunshine.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 11; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. She prizes the stone: never will she venture into the water or drink without first hiding the stone in a safe place, and she is never at rest, glancing back toward it. Whoever finds someone near it she attacks, killing or maiming him for life. If anyone gets the stone without her knowing, he is for his whole life fortunate, loaded with presents; but if she finds the thief, his wife and children die the first day, all his goods vanish, and he wastes away and dies an agonising death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 11; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same locus; not verbatim. A young Bushman of the old race planned to rob the Water-Snake of her stone. He lay hidden under grass and bushes where she buried it, and while she went to bathe he wrapped the stone tight in many things, buried it where she could never find it, and ran home. The snake tracked his spoor to the huts and sniffed through everything; but he had smeared himself with buchu, and she found nothing. He grew rich with presents; but the snake wasted away, the springs ran dry, and he carried the stone back to its hiding-place and told her to come and help him seek for it — where they found it again with great joy. Both were happy thereafter, and the waters returned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories Deel I (1919), No. 11; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun Is the Head of Danser the Fire-Man

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 12

summary.en: The Fire-man's shining head lights the twilight world and takes the hunters' game; the women urge his death. As he crosses the water the arrows bring him down, and the children throw his head into the sky — where it becomes the Sun, seeking its body forever. The body, headless, rots into a crab and still walks the shores at dusk.
summary.zh: 火人明首照微明之世，且奪獵者之獲；婦人慫恿殺之。其涉水時箭下如雨；孩童擲其首上天——遂為日，永尋其軀。無首之軀朽化為蟹，至今黃昏沿岸而行。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
Danser is the Fire-man, the fire-maker. He first walked as a man; light and warmth streamed from his head, for he was the one who placed fire in the stones, in the wood and in the clouds. Where he walked or went there was always light and warmth, so he always had a great company around him: the hunters in his neighbourhood could see where the game was, and those seeking veld food could find it by the light of Danser's head.

But sometimes he was too lazy to walk and sat at ease; when the hunters begged him to go further so they could see the game, he mocked them, asking why they did not go and make light themselves. He also had a way of taking the shot game from the hunters, and the hunters grew angry — for the women are discontented when their men come home without food and have nothing for the hungry children crying for it. So the women advised their men to kill Danser and carry his head round on a long pole, so that everyone might see.

One hunter who liked the women's talk said: 'Good, let us shoot Danser with poisoned arrows, to carry his head on a long pole so we can get warmth and light.' A second said: 'All very well; but whose eyes are tough enough to bear that strong light, and whose hands to cut off that warm head?' A third asked: 'And where do we get a pole that will not burn with the heat?' A fourth said: 'You are bad at making plans! I will tell you what to do: we wait till Danser walks through the water — something he does regularly — then we dart at him with poisoned arrows; if he falls into the water his light and warmth are gone.' A fifth answered: 'You think you are clever, but you are very stupid. Tell me, what good is it to us if Danser's light and warmth are put out? Then we sit in the same old darkness and cold.' But all cried: 'It is nothing! Once he is away from us he can plague and torment us no more.' Lion, leopard, wolf, jackal and cat — men of the old race — wanted nothing to do with the murder; they can see well enough in the dark.

The others kept to their plan. They watched Danser, and just as he stepped through the water they shot, all together; the arrows struck him, he fell forward into the water, and dead was the light and gone the warmth. They ran up, quickly cut off Danser's head under the water, dragged out the body and set the head down on the bank to see what would come of it. But the head and the body would not die: the head's eyes looked round and turned from side to side, and the body stood up and walked about without its head. The head could see and speak but could not move; the body could move but could not see, hear, smell or speak. The head called to the body, but the body did not hear; the body searched for the head but could not find it, and instead of coming nearer walked ever further away.

The murderers went away. Then a girl sent her children to throw the head of Danser into the air so that there should be light and warmth, warning them to beware of the headless body, which would murder them if it caught them. The children stepped carefully; the head was already drying and giving light, and it was so hot when they took hold of it that they threw it into the air at once. Then the mothers cried: 'Wind, Wind, come and take the head high into the blue sky, that we may have light and warmth!' A strong whirlwind came and carried the head above the clouds and let it stay there. The head of Danser the Fire-man became the Sun.

All the people rejoiced that there was now light and warmth over the whole earth: 'O Sun, stay there and give us light and warmth every day... Great is the Sun, who can see all people at once. Now there is light to forbid evil: whoever does evil, steals or murders will be seen, and the Sun will burn him with his heat.' But the head still plays one trick: it seeks for its body. In the morning it climbs, seeking, higher and higher at the mountains on the east side, and when it is high enough sinks again to the mountains on the west, and dives into the deep waters of the sea to seek there too — for the body wasted and rotted and has taken the shape of a Crab. And the body, still headless, walks up and down along the waters at evening, seeking its head.

functions: Cosmogony of the sun as the severed head of the fire-being.
Explains the crab's shape and its dusk patrolling of the shore.
Frames the day-night alternation as the head's endless search.

title.en: The Moon Is the Shoe of the 'Hotnotsgod

region.en: Hantam River & Bushmanland, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省哈坦姆河與布什曼蘭（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition told in Afrikaans; recorded 1870s-1880s by G. R. von Wielligh, published 1919

source.work: G. R. von Wielligh, Boesman-Stories, Deel I (1919), No. 13

summary.en: One of 'Kaggen's shoes, frozen into the Water-Snake's ice and flung into the sky by the wind-bird at the hammerkop's call, becomes the Moon. The Sun melts it to a shoe-sole; the Water-Snake keeps a fountain in the shoe so it refills and freezes; and its moonwater falls as dew. When men see the new moon they cover their eyes and beg to be made like it — dying and living again. Only the Hare's quarrel brings death.
summary.zh: 螳螂之鞋——冰封於水蛇之冰，被風鳥應鎚頭鸛之呼擲上天——化為月。日熔之僅餘鞋底；水蛇於鞋中置泉，水復盈而凍；其月水降為露。人見新月掩目祈曰：使我如月——死而復生。唯野兔之爭帶來死亡。

sensitivity.note: San oral tradition recorded in Afrikaans by G. R. von Wielligh; presented as an archival record.

narrative.en:
The 'Hotnotsgod ('Kaggen) made himself a pair of neat shoes in which he lay dead (i.e. lay still at rest). But one of the shoes — the right — was hard and pressed sore on his right foot; so he told his daughter, the Hammerkop bird, to sit the shoe in the water to soften it. The great Water-Snake was sorely vexed that the 'Hotnotsgod dared put his dirty shoe in the water; she made the water of the dam very cold at night, so that the whole dam froze hard by morning and the shoe sat inside a piece of ice.

That morning the 'Hotnotsgod sent his daughter, the Hammerkop, to fetch the shoe. She brought it with the great shining piece of ice. He was so cross about it that he threw the shoe — up into the air. The Hammerkop, who knows the Wind-bird well, called out: 'Wind-bird, Wind-bird, take the shoe up, up, up into the sky, that we may have light by night too!' A whirlwind came and carried the shoe high into the sky and let it loose there. The shoe with the piece of ice became the Moon.

The Moon with its shining ice began to shine at night, and the people of the old race saw the Moon for the first time. They covered their faces with their hands and praised and honoured the Moon; from then on they had light by night and no longer wandered in the dark — they could hunt aardvark by night and stalk game at the waters and see to shoot it. This the Sun did not like at all, for he wanted to shine alone in the sky; he picked a quarrel with the Moon. The Sun is warm, for he is the head of Danser the Fire-man; the Moon is cold, for he is the frozen waters. So the Sun strove to pour out heat to melt the ice of the Moon. The ice melted, melted, melted until only the sole of the 'Hotnotsgod's shoe was left; and all the people wept that the Moon was now dead.

The great Water-Snake, who cares for the waters of the fountains, heard the weeping and let a fountain come up in the Moon, to make water in the shoe continually, so that the water could become ice. The water in the shoe grew until the whole shoe was full again; the water became ice, and the Moon shone again in full strength. The Sun spat his warm arrows at the Moon again, and the Moon grew smaller and smaller. The melted ice became the night dew, the moonwater; and the bits of ice became the kapok and the frost that falls by night.

When the Bushmen saw the new moon again they covered their eyes with both hands and cried out: 'O Moon, we thought you were altogether dead; but now we see you have come back alive to us. Now we know the Sun will never kill you. You will die, but always come alive again. Make us like you, so that when we grow old we become young again from the beginning and do not die.' And the Moon answered: 'You shall grow old and always grow young again. Therefore you shall never die. When you are old you shall only sleep, and out of that sleep you shall soon wake young again. You shall hunt again, eat and drink again, and your wives and children shall be with you again; for they too shall not die.' So the people of that time never died.

But how did Death come? One evening, as the Moon shone pleasantly, he heard a young man weeping inconsolably. He asked him why he wept so bitterly, and the young man answered: 'My mother is dead, and I shall never see her again.' With deep feeling the Moon said: 'Be comforted, my son. Your mother will come back alive to you. She is only sleeping for a little while, she is not dead.' But the young man strove hard: 'My mother is truly dead; the Wind has gone out of her nostrils and the Fire out of her body, she breathes no more and is stiff and cold.' The Moon comforted him again: 'Look at me: every month I die and quickly come alive again, and so it shall be with all people: they shall only sleep a while and wake again.' But the young man still strove with the Moon, and the Moon grew angry. He gave the young man a blow with the fist on his upper lip, so that the lip split in two, and so the young man changed on the spot into a Hare, which crouches and springs about on the baking-plates in the night and the moonlight. Then the Moon said: 'For your sake I shall curse all the people. Henceforth they shall die and never return to life. But if they do not strive with me, and do not try, like you, to make me a liar, then I shall one day have mercy on all people and raise them out of their graves.' So Death came into the world through the strife of a Hare.

functions: Origin of the moon as the frozen shoe with its fountain of moonwater.
Explains dew, kapok and frost as the melted ice of the moon.
Delivers the death-decree myth in its blessing-curse form.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of von Wielligh Deel I No. 13 (1919); not verbatim. The 'Hotnotsgod made himself neat shoes; one shoe pressed sore on his right foot, so he told his daughter, the Hammerkop bird, to sit the shoe in the water to soften it. The great Water-Snake froze the dam hard; the shoe sat inside a piece of ice; and the 'Hotnotsgod threw the shoe up into the air, where the Wind-bird carried it high at the Hammerkop's call. The shoe with the ice became the Moon.
